title: Trans 101
text:
before I get to the meat of this:

I seem to have some cis straight men following me? Sure. That makes sense, because the way cis straight men seem to make decisions is by following whoever has the hottest take. Like Northernlion. He’s kind of a weird guy actually, but his entire brand is being a married dad and bagging on other weird guys and telling them to be normal, which enables men to claim a kind of superiority-by-proxy.

Mr Lion’s take on AI-generated pornography, for instance, is that it is morally corrupt because it has no soul. This is a perfect take for luring cisgender straight men, who like to believe that they can ethically consume pornography. It is internally consistent and produces surprising results that they can toss around (without necessarily endorsing) in characteristically masculine bids for attention. For instance: this implies that non-AI generated pornography has an intrinsic artisan appeal, and furthermore that certain kinds of pornography, which require more craft, are superior to others1.

In a world where transgender women were prized as they deserve to be, I wouldn’t have to have so many men following me. Because my takes would not be as hot, as defined by their opposition to norms. I guess possibly my Umamusume takes would still attract an audience? But himedanshi aren’t really the demographic I’m talking to here… I guess there are some straight men who treat Oguri Cap like Goku.

Anyways. Cis straight men who aren’t dating transgender women, this one should fit you pretty well.

(trans men I know you want to be included. here.)

* * *

TRANS WOMEN ARE WOMEN, our world proclaimed at the height of peak woke. Which was good. Transgender women are women; this is obvious to anybody who knows one well enough. But nobody actually explained what this meant to most of the populace, because nobody could really explain what a woman is.

You probably can’t either. Which is fine. Womanhood, like art, or sex, is something that most people just intuit based on what people around them do. For instance, a woman usually (but not always) has long hair, acts in feminine ways, is romantically interested in men, enjoys aesthetic curation, and prefers cooperation to competition.

But pattern-matching has its limits, and everybody knows it. Consider a Californian gay man who fulfills all these criteria: not a woman, and if you met him you wouldn’t assume he was. On the other hand, I am obviously a woman and only fill 2.5 of these criteria2, though the pressure of not filling them all does obviously weigh on me.

So then we go to “identity”. It is transparently obvious that “identifying” as a woman is not enough to make somebody a woman, and it is transparently obvious when somebody is making that stupid attack helicopter joke3. What ‘identity’ is actually trying to get at is that if you ask somebody about their gender they will usually tell you, for the same reasons as people will tell you their names. People don’t like to lie about who they truly are4! Consider how men get if you tell them they’re acting like women, or how desperate some nonbinary people are to tell you about their genders. If nobody had any idea what a woman was I would also be regrettably like that.

Feminists used to conceive of womanhood as something that is done to people. This is a very powerful rhetorical tool for building solidarity and showing how ridiculous the world is: compare ‘women are expected to stay in the home and nurture children’, a familiar sentence, to ‘half of humanity is expected to stay in the home and nurture children’. The weakness of this framing, and the reason nobody uses it anymore, is that women by and large don’t want to be referred to as ‘half of humanity’ — we want to be understood to be women, heiresses to a complicated and fraught set of cultural legacies that we are not interested in sweeping under the table.

What nobody wants to say, because nobody but me5 is woke enough to say it, is that the actual nature of womanhood is an immutable spiritual essence, like a kind of ethereal light or glowing liquid, which is then expressed via culturally-modulated principles. This absolutely has some kind of biological correlate but the exact nature of that being proven isn’t something anybody would listen to anyways6.

“Gender isn’t real though!!!” It literally is though. This is how people work — it’s how you work. If gender isn’t real why do you do any of the things you do? Why do you like the things you like? Even in the ways you defy your gender you act according to it. Signs are (typically) arbitrarily assigned — does that mean words aren’t real? And yet you understand what I’m saying. Tangibility has nothing to do with reality; gender, like morality and numbers, is the most real kind of thing there is. You close your eyes to it at your own peril.

Womanhood is a quality that women have within ourselves, and that if properly attuned resonates with the womanhoods of others; the expression of which is governed by the ways the world pushes back on it. As somebody with this quality I can assure you that transgender women have it.

I understand that “it isn’t gay to love trans women” keeps many of you [trans women] safer. but for some of us, it is gay. @halimedemf

It’s true that many women (trans women included) don’t feel like transgender women are women. This is because they’re just pattern-matching. Transgender women aren’t raised as women and so they don’t express womanhood in the ways that being raised as a woman allows — but that doesn’t mean they aren’t women, just that their abilities to express their hearts have been damaged. If you are lucky enough to get to spend time with trans women; if you see how they treat each other, and you, and how they are treated — this beautiful inner light shines through. Maybe it shines through a bit differently, but diversity among women7 is always broader than everyone thinks and should be prized as a marker of a system’s resilience8.

* * *

A parable. Let us define three women Alice, Bella, and Charlotte such that:

Alice is not transgender. But she is sterile, by an accident of genetics. She was raised by a single father with several older brothers. Her father wanted another son, and has made this very clear to her since she was young. She is comparatively tall and comparatively broad of shoulder and flat of chest, and she has been taught none of the feminine skills that would allow her to compensate; therefore she has come to hate her body9. She has an affinity for legible systems, rather than interpersonal communications, and her traumatic youth has caused her to retreat into the areas of her expertise. She is bisexual, and hates herself for being attracted to women. As an adult, she is naturally horrifically jealous of other women, and develops uncomfortable fetishes around being made to wear dresses and so forth.

Now: is Alice transgender? No, definitionally, even if she experiences the results of transmisogyny because people think she is. But is there compassion for her, in your heart? How is she different from you? How is she the same?

Bella has a supportive family — and most critically, a supportive mother. She is encouraged as a child to present and act as she pleases, and when she insists for over a year that she is a girl her mother believes her and takes her to a doctor, where steps are taken to ensure she can undergo the puberty that fits her best. She doesn’t have periods, but she does have supportive peer groups and adults in her life who care about her for who she is, and consequently developed “only” the normal body issues of a girl in her teens. She is bisexual, and normal about it, or as normal about it as anybody bisexual can be10. As an adult, she naturally feels more comfortable around other women, and has a fairly normal sex life, though she’s really into feet for some reason. It happens.

Now: is Bella transgender? Yes, definitionally, even if she doesn’t experience the results of transmisogyny because nobody knows she is. She happens to be transgender, but that mostly matters in bed; in fact, she plays it down a lot of the time as a matter of safety, shame, and awkwardness. (I’ve met girls like Bella. There are more out there than you think.) What pressures are acting on her? How is she lucky, or unlucky, to conform in such ways?

Charlotte has never gotten along with her family. She is forced to be a woman in the way her mother was forced to be a woman, and her mother before her. When she is seven she looks out a window and sees how free boys get to be and something ugly twists inside her. She is not a boy but she wants that freedom. She likes dresses, or at least she likes how people treat her when she wears them; she undergoes the pain of menarche and the bitterness of pretending that nothing in her body is hurting her, that nothing has happened; she is raised to be married to a man and have children because that’s what happened to her mother and so that’s what will happen to her. She is treated as a childbearing body; an object. She has a normal girl’s body, insofar as such a thing could be said to exist. Some parts of her are recognized as woman-befitting. The parts that are not bring her pain. She is bisexual but finds it easier to date men than women: there are many more of them and being “one of the boys” is easier for her than admitting that she doesn’t always get along with other women. As an adult she is bitter. One day, after a few drinks, she confesses to her friend Bella that she hates her coworker, a woman named Alice, because Alice is “obviously” a man pretending to be a woman. Bella is never quite as good of a friend to her, after that. She thinks this is because Bella has been corrupted by wokeness, and starts posting terribly online.

Now: while Charlotte is not transgender, there are many ways in which she is like a transgender woman. How much compassion do you feel she deserves? More or less than Alice? Than Bella? Than a transgender woman in her place? How is her case different from transgender infighting? How is it similar?

Yes, transgender women are often weird and offputting — weirder in many cases than non-trans women, who have often been raised in ways that make it clear that deviance from consensus will be punished; offputting because abuse doesn’t make victims nice to be around and transgender women are practically always child abused. There’s resentment on both sides: transgender women see non-trans women as having something they desperately want, and insufficiently-enlightened cisgender women see trans women as wanting something they have complicated gross feelings about.

Ultimately all I can say is that I myself am a woman who will not obey many of the strictures of womanhood but a woman nonetheless, and that trans women are, in my experience, the same. Or more even.

If a woman is somebody who struggles under the yoke of womanhood and does not shirk from it, trans women are the women of women.

You could just bookmark my substack, but wouldn’t you prefer to also get my emails? to pay me dollars monies for them, even?

title: Mobile Suit Gundam Watch Order
text:
You want to get into Gundam? How much time do you have?

43 episodes worth? Okay great. Start with Mobile Suit Gundam.

Maybe enough for like, six episodes? You can watch the first six episodes of Mobile Suit Gundam. or the movies for Mobile Suit Gundam. or 0080 War In The Pocket.

Maybe like one episode? Watch Episode 1 of Mobile Suit Gundam. Or the prologue to Witch From Mercury, I guess.

One trailer? Here.

* * *

Great. Now that everybody who hasn’t watched Mobile Suit Gundam yet is busy watching Mobile Suit Gundam, HERE is my recommended watch order. For all of you who’ve already seen it, to argue about.

I. Adolescence (who are we?)

Mobile Suit Gundam - psychic self-mutiliation1

Mobile Suit Zeta Gundam - bellum iustum

Iron-Blooded Orphans - bellum se ipsum alit

Char’s Counterattack - 無理心中 (muri-shinju; forced double murder-suicide, typically between lovers)

II - Love (what good is it?)

08th MS Team (1, 4-11) - star-crossed lovers

and/or

The Witch From Mercury (prologue - 12, S2 ED) - the delicate touch of a lesbian

III. Adulthood (how do we live in an evil world?)

Victory Gundam - don’t stop! carry on!

Hathaway’s Flash - they walk ahead into the darkness, and they do not come back.

Stardust Memory (as much as you can stomach) - passionate intensity

IV. Ɐ

Turn A Gundam - for all given

Appendix

six-episode OVA War In The Pocket is just straightforwardly excellent, and can be watched at any point — though it benefits from having finished the original series.

* * *

I. ADOLESCENCE // Who are we?

Mobile Suit Gundam (43 episodes)

It is the year 0079 of the Universal Century. A half-century has passed since Earth began moving its burgeoning population into gigantic orbiting space colonies. A new home for mankind, where people are born and raised. And die.

War is hell. Fifteen-year-old Amuro Ray is press-ganged into the Earth Federation’s war to keep the fascist Duchy of Zeon from escaping their control. He pilots the Gundam, a prototype armored mech designed by his father to kill anything it can hit. Don’t look back, Amuro. Men don’t show their tears.

Every other Gundam is a reaction to the situation this one presents: you can try to invent or love your way out2; you can come to enjoy the killing3; you can try to end all war by getting stronger and killing more people4; you can stop feeling bad about it5; you can become an ecoterrorist6, or a slightly worse ecoterrorist7; you can be a good little soldier who does as she’s told8. Amuro tries defiance; he tries to run; he tries in vain to resist the forces molding him into a man, a thing made to kill. None of it works.

First Gundam isn’t well-animated by modern standards, but the writing is good and the colors are gorgeous. Yes there are movie versions but you really should watch the whole series. Transgender women love this show because it’s about how masculinity turns children into monsters. Fujoshi love this show because it’s about a boy with a slim little waist being tortured into an eating disorder. You want to think about Char Aznable forever, right? The two problems with watching this are that you will never stop thinking about Char Aznable and you will get very annoyed with people who say Evangelion is the first serious mech show9.

A Gundam is a mask of metal manhood that takes all punishment. A Gundam enables you to kill. A Gundam is a coffin.

yaoi score 7 (Charma is so important)

women score 4 (would be lower but people forget about Mirai using Sayla as her substitute boyfriend)

cuckolding: yes.

horrors of war: Tomino was a child during WWII, and has memories of hiding in air raid shelters. it shows.

Mobile Suit Zeta Gundam (50 episodes)

Universal Century 0087. Seven years after the end of the One Year War, the Titans, an elite Federation counter-insurgency unit tasked with eliminating the remnants of Zeon, have seized control of the space colonies. Those who object to their rule are labeled Zeon sympathizers and killed. Against them stands the Anti-Earth Union Group, a scrappy terrorist collective of former Zeon and Earth Federation troops. But the asteroid base Axis, where Zeon’s remaining fleet have spent the past seven years hungering for revenge, has set course for Earth orbit…

War is evil — and yet some wars must be fought. Fascism must be stopped. And so seventeen-year-old prodigy Kamille Bidan is press-ganged by the AEUG into its war against the Titans. His Zeta Gundam represents his own potential to fly past human limits. Zeon’s ideology predicts that spaceborn children will become a new type of human capable of understanding others without misconceptions — but Titans, AEUG, and Axis Zeon alike all realize that being able to feel other’s souls makes you really good at aiming at them. The transcendent gift that was supposed to end all conflict becomes just another way for people to kill each other.

Yes, to Zeta-era!Tomino women are a kind of animal that eat men to survive; yes, Rosamia Badam is painful to watch; yes, the middle of the show drags. This is still the only Gundam that has made me cry. Over a straight couple, even, as Kamille Bidan and doomed psychic Four Murasame find themselves drawn to each other and torn apart by forces beyond their control. (The despicable Paptimus Srirocco is a direct ancestor to Akio Ohtori — and Sarah Zabiarov’s hair is pink! If you watch this and the original Gundam you will recognize some of the seeds of Revolutionary Girl Utena.) There are compilation movies; skip them10.

A Gundam transforms. Amuro was an ordinary boy, but Kamille is a prodigy; it doesn’t matter. A Gundam holds the hopes of the future — of technology, of space exploration, of a better world — and it represents the total annihilation of those hopes when the form of freedom is used to kill.

yaoi score 7 (tomino was the first one on the Charmuro train. The key to Quattro/Kamille is that Kamille has Garma’s hair)

women score 6 (lots of them. some good; some terrible. Kamille is named after Camille Claudel — and NOT a woman but he is narratively feminized)

cuckolding: yes

horrors of war: entire space colonies get gassed.

Mobile Suit ZZ Gundam

Mobile Suit Gundam: Iron-Blooded Orphans (50 episodes)

323 years Post Disaster —

Wait! Isn’t this spot supposed to go to Mobile Suit ZZ Gundam? The show directly after Zeta, featuring many of the same characters?

No, because ZZ Gundam isn’t as funny as Iron-Blooded Orphans. And also I hate it.

Zeta Gundam stands for Z, the final letter of our alphabet; the end of all hope and potential. ZZ is what comes after. The next generation, a squad of carefree child soldiers, will grow up in a parched dead world where they will kill until they die.

ZZ’s Judau Ashta and his sociopathic little gang of looters cannot lose. Nothing means anything anymore. Haman Karn, the only women with any dignity in Zeta, loses her composure lusting over a fourteen year old; Ple clones die and get replaced; Judau’s little sister Leina dies and he just keeps going (and then she’s alive, because nothing matters) — Judau Ashta will just keep killing and making silly faces forever and nothing will ever change.

Sure they get up to goofy antics but ZZ completely fails to understand military homoeroticism. IBO is one big sick joke: for example, Tekkadan’s success as child soldiers leads to measurable increases in child soldier use, as militaries realize that children’s neuroplasticity makes them really good candidates for the life-threatening spinal implants used to control mobile suits.

Besides: thematically we need to see the kind of world that would cause Char Aznable to go on to do All That, and After War X isn’t willing to kill off any of its main characters, and IBO is retroactively tied to Turn A.

So.

323 years Post Disaster. The Earth, scarred by war on an unfathomable scale, exists in an uneasy compromise secured by peacekeeping organization Gjallerhorn. On Mars, a group of child soldiers revolt against their owners and rename themselves Tekkadan, an independent paramilitary organization. Their first contract: bring a rich girl inciting revolution to Earth, directly under Gjallerhorn’s nose.

War is all there is. The orphans of Tekkadan know nothing but kill or be killed and they are going to kill until they die — unfortunately for everyone and everything else they are very very good at killing. Mad dog Mikazuki Augus pilots the bestial Gundam Barbatos11 via spinal implant.

There’s a lull after the opening episodes but it’s worth it. Mari Okada is in full form here, and her obsessions with child abuse, cuckolding, and resentment dovetail nicely with Tomino’s precedents. I love Kudelia (of course) and Yamagi (of course) but McGillis Fareed steals the show as my personal second favorite Gundam Blonde Man Who Causes Problems behind only Char Aznable. Skip the movie of the mobile game.

A Gundam is a demon. A Gundam is a rabid beast that needs to be put down.

yaoi score 10. thank you Mari Okada for Mikazuki’s 24/7 bdsm dynamic with Orga.

women score 4. nobody talks about fumitan :( two of them do get married though, and points to Azee for getting the Hat of Harem Leadership

cuckolding: yes

horrors of war: hyperviolence.

Mobile Suit Gundam: Char’s Counterattack (1 movie)

Universal Century 0093. Amuro’s ex old rival Char Aznable has taken control of Neo Zeon and declared war on the Earth Federation for their crimes against the planet. He has begun dropping asteroids on Earth, with the express and stated intent of killing every last person remaining there.

The world is completely and irredeemably fucked. The Earth Federation’s tyranny has gone too long unchecked; even in space, humanity is choked by Earth’s gravity. And so the Earth must be cleansed. Amuro Ray never does realize that his last words to Char in Zeta kicked all this off, but he gets back in a Gundam, convinced that if he can just beat some sense into that idiot Char he’ll stop trying to kill everybody on Earth.

It seems complicated but honestly it explains itself. CCA is maybe the most psychosexually loaded work in an extremely psychosexually potent series. There’re some really wild quotes in this one. “They say Commander Char is a lolicon” is only like the third most out there line in this movie, to be clear. Oh, and keep an eye on Hathaway Noa for later.

A Gundam holds the power of the way things were. A Gundam has the funnels — her weapons. Do you remember when we drew our swords, foreheads pressed together in the ecstasy of violence, and marked each other’s bodies irrevocably? A Gundam can save us. Love — however blind and misguided — can save us. We can pass on together.

yaoi score: unfathomable. go read the lyrics to Beyond The Time.

women score: 6. quess paraya haters are wrong. as a newtype she’s just saying what the people around her don’t want to admit they already think. nanai miguel I love you

cuckolding: literally every single character in this entire movie is getting cuckolded; over half of them are being cuckolded multiple times over.

horrors of war: absolutely.

* * *

II. LOVE // what good is it?

The 08th MS Team (Episodes 1, 4-11)

Universal Century 0079. Federation and Zeon troops wage guerrilla war on the Southeast Asian front. As the Federation’s Gundams push deeper into the jungle, Zeon tests the Apsalus, a superweapon with the potential to turn the tide of the war…

There is a place for humanity, even on the battlefield. Ensign Shiro Amada and test pilot Aina Sahalin discover that their real loyalties lie with each other, over family, command, and moral compunctions.

Yes, everybody knows how well-animated that Gouf fight is, but my favorite scene is the one in episode 7 where Shiro and Aina use the Gundam, a body built for war, to heat water for a bath. I’ve cut episodes 2 and 3 to balance Shiro and Aina a little more, and because the early episodes really grate after seeing how competent he is in the first. Honestly you could cut up to 6. Episode 12 is just no good, and they were right to leave it out of the American broadcast.

A Gundam is a body clinging to another. A Gundam is a mask that allows you to kill. If you stop being able to kill, and you lose that mask’s protection, you won’t be able to survive.

But there are things more important than living.

yaoi score 0 (maybe you could do something with Ginias and Norris?)

women score 5 (thank you Karen Joshua. I wish Aina was more of a character.)

cuckolding: Ginias is a little too invested in controlling his sister.

horrors of war: intent to rape, for one.

and/or:

The Witch From Mercury (prologue - 12, S2 ED)

Ad Stella 122. GUND-ARM technology was created to help humans survive in space, and those who created it built Gundams to defend themselves. What controls a prosthesis can just as easily control a mobile suit. The democratization of violence that Gundams represent has been banned, but the megacorporations that rule the Earth Sphere are hungry for profits.

Miorine Rembran’s father has forced her engagement to whoever wins mobile suit duels. Transfer student Suletta Mercury is a very good girl who knows how to do exactly one thing: win mobile suit duels. Love — romantic or familial — doesn’t always make us better. Sometimes it makes us worse.

Fans of Revolutionary Girl Utena will appreciate this one, as will fans with fuller Gundam literacy. Belmeria Winston as Monica Arno is an excellent deep cut. Unfortunately, they went too far with the references and turned the ending of this one into Unicorn. You can watch season 2 if you want but don’t say I didn’t warn you; the credits sequence is admittedly gorgeous. Someday we’re going to get the story of what happened behind the scenes to cause such a mess.

Aerial’s design is sporty and feminine and nonthreatening. We like to pretend, with “sports” and “regulations” and “honor” and “cute girl”s, that a Gundam is not a hideous and evil thing — but a Gundam is a body capable of killing. Forget this at your peril.

yaoi score 4 (sometimes I feel like the world’s only non-Japanese Guel/Shaddiq shipper)

women score 10

cuckolding: of course.

horrors of war: once, and only once, though the show first bares its teeth whenever Happy Birthday plays. but what a once it is.

* * *

III. ADULTHOOD // how do we live in an evil world?

Victory Gundam (51 episodes)

Universal Century 0153. The Federation’s decline has left a power vacuum that the Zanscare Empire is all too eager to fill. Those who oppose them face the guillotine. The understaffed League Militaire, a desperate band of resistance fighters, tries to buy time for the Federation to mobilize the resources it has left.

Thirteen year old Uso Ewin finds himself fighting on the front lines — the League Militaire has nobody else. Only one person sees how ridiculous this is, and her frustration with the League’s willingness to use child soldiers drives her right into Zanscare’s waiting arms…

Uso is to this day the single Gundam protagonist with the highest on-screen kill count12. He just keeps killing and killing and killing. Somebody’s got to do it. It doesn’t matter how many ill-fated women die, or how many Freudian torments he is subjected to: Uso Ewin is a machine. If he ever broke, or even stopped, the story would end. This doesn’t actually make him particularly fun to watch, but there is something very awful/funny about a thirteen-going-on-forty year old with a wife and child picking up his briefcase and straightening his tie to go to war.

A Gundam is the sword of the downtrodden. Against some forces, the power to kill is the only hope people have. Do not be fooled into thinking that that makes it a good thing.

yaoi score 0

women score: minus points for misogyny but it’s definitely got some. Katejina Loos may perhaps have done some things wrong.

cuckolding: yes.

horrors of war: ohhh boy.

Hathaway’s Flash (Two movies for now; a third one eventually)

Universal Century 0105. The Federation defiles the Earth and oppresses its people, deploying mobile suits into cities under the pretext of immigration control. Ecoterrorist Mafty Navue Erin has issued an ultimatum: his organization will kill Earth Federation ministers until and unless every single human being alive has left Earth for the colonies.

Mafty Navue Erin is actually Hathaway Noa (yes, that Hathaway Noa), now a quiet young botanist driven to obsession by the death of Quess Paraya. A chance hijacking leaves him entangled with Colonel Kenneth Sleg, the leader of an anti-Mafty task force, and Gigi Andalucia, a Federation official’s consort who realizes his secret identity.

Some people look at the world and close their eyes to suffering. Some people look at the world and become vegetarian, or vegan even. Some people look at the world and dedicate their entire lives to waging unwinnable war, because there’s no other way they could live with themselves. The world is too rotten. Somebody has to do something NOW.

Pity the poor noble fools.

These movies are trying to be Mature And Serious Gundam For Adults13. Pros of this approach: the photorealistic environments are dizzying; Hathaway spends a lot of time gripping his thighs in sexual torment as Kenneth and Gigi parade their bodies in front of him (this is very funny to me). Cons of this approach: the fight scenes at night are barely legible (the Messers in the first movie aside. I love the way that they light palm trees on fire); the Xi Gundam’s ridiculous design is taken completely seriously.

I do like how petty and libidinal everyone is: Gigi’s patron explains almost apologetically that he can do the work he does because he rewards himself with her body; men and women alike in Hathaway’s crew go topless while he self-flagellates in the shower over his inability to escape lust; one rebel faction is convinced that their footage of atrocity is going to mobilize all of humanity to overthrow the Earth Federation if they can just get it on television. Tomino goes after leftists like only leftists can.

A Gundam is a legacy. A Gundam makes you look ridiculous. A Gundam is a weight on your shoulders that compels you to get yourself killed.

yaoi score 6. Kenneth Sleg wants Hathaway on his lap so bad, and he takes his frustrations at not having him out on poor Lain Aim with that riding crop

women score: Gigi Andalucia’s redecorating montage is absolutely critical to the work. Hathaway does slutshame somebody but he’s pretty clearly in the wrong.

cuckolding: every single character. Tomino’s in full form here.

horrors of war: yes.

Stardust Memory (as much as you can stomach)

Universal Century 0083. The Federation has grown complacent — and the remnants of Zeon have stolen a prototype Gundam equipped with a nuclear bomb.

This is the alternative to Hathaway’s Flash: a world where nobody stands for anything. The Federation is barely functional; the Delaz Fleet is a reactionary mess; Cima Garahau’s fleet and Anaheim Electronics only care about profit. Nobody in Stardust Memory believes in anything but power. No wonder all of Kou’s crewmates join the Titans. Take heart in the fact that Kamille probably blew them up! The animation is beautiful, at least. Watch until you’re sick of these people — that may be in like two episodes, or less.

A Gundam has a nuke.

yaoi score: 2. surprisingly low for all the homofascism.

women score: Nina is so cute. It’s a shame about. all that. Mora Boscht :)

cuckolding: causes so many problems in this one.

horrors of war: mass starvation. a space colony, dropped on the Earth

* * *

IV. Ɐ // and now what?

Turn A Gundam (50 episodes)

It is the year 2345 of the Correct Century. Millennia have passed since the Moonrace left Earth, and only now, under Queen Dianna Soreil, will they return to mankind’s birthplace.

Their technology is undeniably superior. A single Moonrace mobile suit can easily destroy cities; the peoples of Earth have only myths of the ages when giant metal men waged war with technologies they can no longer even conceptualize. The Earthlings have lost their history, their culture, and their weapons. They are weak, fractured, and clueless.

But Queen Dianna Soreil refuses to let her people take what is rightfully theirs. She insists they negotiate with Earth’s squabbling children, who have only just rediscovered the telephone, as equals. Resentment grows: why is she humoring these idiot primitives? Our ancestors left this planet to save it; to let it regrow from the ravages of war and pollution, and now the Earthlings grow fat on milk and honey. The land is ours.

Again and again, the Queen sues for peace. Her people chew their stale rations while they stare at fields of ripe grain.

War is inevitable.

But Loran Cehack, a Moonrace scout sent to assess the planet’s suitability, defects. He loves the Earth, and Queen Diana, and he declares his intention to fight anyone who doesn’t value human life, even his own people.

He has discovered something that should never have been unearthed: a Gundam more dangerous than nuclear fire.

At the end of all timelines, the Turn A awaits…

Turn A Gundam is about the necessity of striving for peace, no matter how stupid and arduous and pointless the process of that striving feels. Turn A Gundam is about the value of even a single human life.

A Gundam is an answer.

women score: unfathomable, for the same reason as CCA’s yaoi score

horrors of war: as much as people try to avoid them, nuclear bombs are in play and at least one goes off.

title: WARHOUND and the transfeminine psyche
text:
CONTENT WARNING: discussion of canon-typical sexual violence. It’s kind of what the whole thing is about.

* * *

If you don’t already know what WARHOUND is you don’t spend a lot of time around a certain kind of gay early 20s transgender women. Basically it’s about what if a woman mech pilot was sexually treated like a dog, and trans is very into that. It is currently spawning an entire transgender post-Empty Spaces microgenre about this.

Anyways people get very upset about WARHOUND, for many reasons: they don’t think women should be treated like dogs; they find the whole thing depressing; they feel like Kallidora Rho is working in a genre and context that she isn’t sufficiently engaged with; they hate women.

I happen to agree with some of their criticisms. I find Rho’s prose lacking; I think WARHOUND isn’t a very context-grounded work; I think that Ancyor isn’t a very interesting mech for a story to which the mech-as-power-fantasy is critical. But the prose is not the point! The worldbuilding or lack thereof is not the point. WARHOUND is not about any of those other things, and analyzing it through those lenses isn’t going to get you anywhere, because WARHOUND is pornography — and the telos of pornography is pure stimulation. Here are WARHOUND’s stimuli: the thrill of skill and power suborned to an eroticized fear of bestial debasement, the supremacy of control over desire, and also lots of getting punched in the stomach.

No wonder trans women love this so much.

The value of WARHOUND, then, is in what it can tell us about the kinds of pornography trans seeks out and creates, and the antecedent transgender neuroses which cause her to do so.

As previously discussed, the upbringing transgender women are forced through, while it does permanently damage her, at least allows her expertise and a defiant joy in testing her own limits through competition. She is aware, however, that this is not an opportunity often afforded to her counterpart non-trans women, and therefore often develops a complex of guilt around it. This complex is part of why trans women are so drawn to WARHOUND: it posits that she can atone for her prowess, which she feels she is somehow unwomanly of her, through debasement and sexual subservience.

Sarthra Thrace performs her unfeminine display of physical prowess as ordered by her Handler, who controls and rewards her, treating her like a dog sexually. The fear of deviation from womanhood is assuaged by her lack of agency — Handler is making her do this, so she doesn’t need to be ashamed of it.

And then this fear of deviation from womanhood is deliberately stoked, and stoked, and assuaged again. WARHOUND is pornography. She is made to betray her allies; to be debased with various bodily fluids; to be sexually available to whomever her Handler wishes. Of course she does not want these things1. But anybody who has studied or been subject to power knows that control is only real insofar as the subject can be made to do things against some part of their own will. The subject is only controlled insofar as she is made to abandon and defile her former principles as a demonstration of the supremacy of that control and of her own abjection.

Desire = Weakness = Animal Nature < Control = Strength = Inhumanity. Yes this is reiterated endlessly but that’s the point. It’s pornography. That single line about the Handler not drinking takes on more and more importance as the story goes on. (I did like Kione Monax developing an eating disorder.)

By being made into a creature that exists to only to fight she flirts with the fear of detransition — of being perceived as an actor rather than an object; a man rather than a woman. We all know dogs are the boy animal. But this, too, WARHOUND answers: It’s fine. It wasn’t really her fault. She is not and never can be a man because she is treated as something fundamentally feminine; ie, subjugated. She is being controlled hard enough to erase her complicity, isn’t she. (isn’t she? well, yes. you shouldn’t blame her, at any rate.)

So what is the side being turned on? You may notice that the entire rebellion is made up of queer women, and that all three protagonists are alienated from it: Sartha is crushed by expectations; Kione is a mercenary2; Leinth is canonically trans.

(Imperials are also shown mostly to be women but Leinth considers it worthy of thought that a female pilot is groping her; we also see a man or two as gerontocrats in SHOWHOUND, though those men are probably gay. We are meant to understand that men are around but not really sexually involved, except as groping hands and phalluses, if Handler deems it appropriate. This is because Kallidora prefers women sexually. Which is quite a reasonable preference.)

Sartha Thrace is in a trans woman’s position: held up as a banner, lauded for her accomplishments, effectively abandoned by those who should be her community. No wonder so many people thrill at the chance to rape and debase her. The Handler is at least honest about her desire to do so: the trans woman is a woman. That’s why she’s subjugated. As a trans woman — as a woman — as a human — she has desires and those desires are a perfect handle for the Handler to judo flip break her spine.

WARHOUND would be completely unrecognizable in a world where transgender women felt accepted.

* * *

MECHA INTERLUDE

Mechsploitation’s roots in Armored Core VI’s story trailer are clear, but we can go deeper.

This is obvious to anybody who has watched a Gundam (Evangelion counts) and has a brain, but it still bears saying: a giant robot is a body that conveys a relationship to force. Cyber Newtype Four Murasame’s Psyco Gundam externalizes her mental instability into indiscriminate civilian casualties3; neural damage from Mikazuki Augus’ spinal-port connection to Gundam Barbatos leaves him hemipelagic4, and incapable of civilian life; Eva-01’s Berserk Mode is diagetically Yui but functions thematically as the release of Shinji’s own repressed rage5.

Whether or not Kallidora Rho is familiar with these sources6, they color the informed reader’s perception of Ancyor. Ancyor is a mobile melee fighter consistently referred to in animalistic terms. That’s a very “cool” thing to be. It could be even “cooler” if she fleshed it out more, even if I know Kallidora only intended to paint it impressionistically. Yes, very few people have ever had the opportunity to pilot post-Cold War so I can’t really fault her for not having any practical experience. To her credit she does move further in this direction with Theaboros Archon. Personally I find that pornographic material is much stronger firmly embedded in a context. But that’s just my own sexual preferences, which I will write an article about some other time.

* * *

OKAY BACK TO THE SPLOITATION

I’ve been trying to meet this text on its own terms, but I just don’t have the thing that makes me afraid of being a violent monster attacking my former comrades-in-arms.

This probably sounds like I think I’m better than that. Like I think I would never betray my principles. But I’m not so arrogant. If you tortured me enough you could probably get me to say or do anything — although, I must note, if anybody were to resort to torture to force me to commit transphobia, or any other bigotries, they would by doing so have admitted that they lost the true battle, of rhetorics.

I’m fit enough, if only because my older sister is running marathons now and I can do anything she can. I jog sometimes; I walk a lot. I am a performer, and performance demands skill. I’m competitive, if not usually in the same arenas as transgender women are. I do a lot of work to be at least competent at anything I try, and I do it successfully. As a femme I have complicated feelings on womanhood and deviation and appropriation and assimilation.

I think (I hope) a lot of trans women can relate to a lot of that. Or some of you, to some of it. We’re women, trans and cis alike.

I mean, I understand the fear of public humiliation. I understand the fear of rape. I understand the fear of having the girl you love most in the world walk out on you during your anniversary dinner because she saw a flash of black hair. Those things don’t necessarily have to have happened to me for me to fear them, but they are possibilities that I have at least considered. I’m just not afraid of being turned into a violent monster and attacking my previous peers for the same reason I’m not scared of, I don’t know, having a tree grow out of my nose. I haven’t had the life context that would make me aware that that would even be something to be scared of. WARHOUND’s fanbase indicates that many transgender women have.

That scares me.

Also I don’t like it when girls get punched in the stomach. That makes me feel gross.

* * *

title: serially published trans-woman-relevant fiction
text:
I like serial longform fiction. I like getting a little notification and settling in to read a little more of a story. Maybe I’m still chasing the high of Homestuck upd8s, but even if it doesn’t change the story itself, stretching it out it changes the reflection of it in the reader’s mind. There’s more to interface with; more to immerse yourself in.

I also like transgender women, and I’m interested in the complexes and neuroses that transgender women often develop. I feel like longform serial work is uniquely suited to getting into transgender women’s heads because of its ability to portray the awful lengthy grind done to her, as her living her whole life…

Though the following works are not necessarily by or even solely about transgender women, they do all get at facets of what transgender women (and non-transgender women) experience. Transgender women may feel seen by the works on this list; non-transgender women can, I hope, gain some measure of insight into what it must be like to be one of them.

(light spoilers follow)

* * *

The Flower That Bloomed Nowhere - Lurina

paranoia, guilt, violation, passing.

Utsushikome of Fusai is hiding a sin that makes it impossible for her to kill herself; she lives in the worst possible world for a girl with her particular neuroses. Also this is a mystery novel — specifically a When They Cry.

Su’s particular flavors of jealousy and jaded self-hatred read as extremely transgender, as do the conditions around “assimilation failure” and the resulting “witches”. A few years ago a cis woman I follow posted about her sexual fascination with her transgender wife’s orgasms - all that effort for the tiniest little precious pearl of liquid. That’s what The Flower That Bloomed Nowhere’s yuri is like.

* * *

Coquette Dragoon - Ivy May

militarization, alienation, agency and coping mechanisms

A sad little bunny signs up to go to Gundam war. Yes the author has decided to market it as The Ageplay And Pee VN but actually it’s about shame and complicity and how girls react to the realities of power. And those other things I guess. This one is very much a Gundam and comes with Gundam-typical warnings (eating disorders, violent deaths, evil boys). A lot of recent Gundam unfortunately fails to grapple with the sheer difficulty of killing another person, even in a military context, and the resulting consequences —but I have no worry that Coquette Dragoon will treat life and the loss thereof with anything less than the reverence and horror it deserves.

Girls who the world tries to turn into men end up obsessed with their abilities to cause harm. Sweet scared little Xiomara could kill somebody, you know. She could get in her Coquette Dragoon and end a human life. She’d get over it, too, eventually. That’s the really awful thing. Transgender women are put in situations that teach them that not having that power is worse, which is part of why they’re like that.

* * *

Unarchived - bb wolfclaw

defiance, other faces, sexuality and need entangled, mommy issues

Three vtubers destroy their careers over each other. One of them is employed; one of them is a former idol; one of them is transgender. This one has just gotten started and I’m very much looking forward to seeing where it goes.

Positioning the trans woman as the one mothering her own mother (the kind of woman situation that readers associate with cis women) is an extremely strong move on the author’s part. Not that Eden’s transness is minimized — just that it’s treated as the cause of problems she has of ≅ equal magnitude to Jun’s and Sierra’s. Transgender women are women, and that means that they have women’s problems, and that’s something that quite a lot of people (many of them transgender women) need to get into their heads.

* * *

Misericorde - xeecee

isolation, religious psychosis, libidinal mania, nuns

As an Anchoress, Hedwig was supposed to spend her entire life in her cell — but there’s been a murder and the Abbess has nobody else with a solid alibi. Also a When They Cry.

The relevance to trans women here is Hedwig’s isolation, particularly as a woman isolated from other women. Of course she’s ludicrously horny — if she had internet access she’d be posting about it, but she doesn’t so there’s really only the one way for her to let off steam. Understandable even if I had to take frequent breaks because I’m too empathetic to enjoy cringe comedy, even when it’s very intentional.

* * *

WARHOUND and sequels - Kallidora Rho

supremacy of control over desire, weakness and weaponhood, internality, force.

I have a lot to say about the things this one reveals about the transgender psyche. Actually I have so much that I will just write an entire other article about it.

* * *

What Happens Next - Max Graves

masculinity, agency, culpability

A weird sad guy raised as a girl suffers the fallout of his best friend’s murder spree.

Max (a longtime associate of mine) is interested in guys who have something wrong with them. Transgender women in What Happens Next exist as a counterpoint — people who were also raised in the wrong gender role but are willing to bite down and face their problems. Vikki in particular is a very good depiction of the ways that living as a transgender woman pushes them to snap, and also a genuinely decent person who isn’t going to be able to fix the current situation. I think that’s a very charitable take on transgender women and I wish more of you held it as aspirational.

* * *

O Human Star - Blue Delliquanti

potential, forking paths, legacy, absolution.

Sixteen years after his death, resurrected roboticist Alistair Sterling finds his old partner raising a robot girl who looks suspiciously like he does.

Sulla contends with being made in the image of somebody she has never known and passing as human in a world that isn’t ready for her; Alistair contends with discovering he has something like a daughter. I think, though, that the most important thing here is something I’ve been trying to get across: sometimes people who are not trans women care about you and have interesting things to say about you respectfully. Maybe you’ll listen if somebody who isn’t me demonstrates that.

* * *

Halimarriede’s Substack - “Halimarriede”

Some transgender lesbian is writing about being Halimede. Curious about where this one is going.

Transgender women are women, and can do all kinds of things. Pretending to be somebody you aren’t, though, can be dangerous. You’d think they would learn that from the testosterone.

* * *

title: The Penis Monologues: Because She Liked To Look At It
text:
Previously: A Part At The Seam: Recognizing Difference Between Cis And Trans Women, Halimede.

Context: The Vagina Monologues, V. Specifically This One

* * *

Content Warning: The Vagina Monologues-typical frank discussion of body shaming, rape, self-harm, etc.

* * *

BECAUSE SHE LIKED TO LOOK AT IT

(the speaker is a transgender woman. There’s a lot of fun staging you could do here but: it is critical that either she should be differentiated from the other women who have performed their monologues or she should not. of course in every work the actor can technically assert final say but in this particular Vagina Monologue — or rather, Penis Monologue — the actress must be as free as possible to color as she will.)

This is how I came to love my penis.

It’s embarrassing because transgender women are supposed to hate every part of ourselves. Women are taught that they’re lower than men; transgender women are taught that we’re lower than women. If you hate your body enough,

if you starve yourself enough

if you cut yourself enough

That suffering doesn’t mean enough to make you a real woman, just a faggot. Every cis woman thinks of herself as a victim, and you’re not going to change that just by having it worse than her. But if you hurt yourself enough some of them might recognize that you are more of a woman than all the other freaks, at least. Enough that somebody might pity you enough to fuck you.

I know loving a penis is like the least feminist thing imaginable. The Vagina Monologues is a deeply personal work compiled from years of interviews with women who were taught to hate their own bodies; The Penis Monologues is a punchline. A woman’s vagina is a locus of desire and repression and disgust and pleasure and freedom; we develop complexes and collect interviews and write plays about it. Nobody needs to tell men to love their penises. Has a man ever had a complicated opinion about his penis? Maybe if it’s small, he wishes it was bigger. Maybe if it’s too big, like, so big it’s inconvenient, he wishes it was smaller. Maybe he has a fetish for having a big or small penis. That’s it, really.

The word vagina is from the, Latin for scabbard; where a weapon is placed.

Did you know what is done to us, cis women? They pick out some girls when we are young, because we have penises like they do, and they turn us into weapons to keep the rest of you in line. Those who do not comply — who dare to show softness, weakness, kindness — get beaten and raped, just like you. You are taught that a part of yourself is filthy; we are taught that the purpose of a penis is force.

In high school my best friend and I were in love. We were making out in the back of my car and her hand went down, down between my legs; grasping softly and then with confusion; desperation. She started crying when she found out I wasn’t hard. She thought I didn’t want her. That there was something wrong with her.

So I told her I was gay.

“Why didn’t you tell me,” she said. She was the president of the GSA. “It makes sense. You were always so nice… I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have pressured you into this.”

We stopped being friends after that.

I know the story. Trans bodies are beautiful: my self-hatred is only the internalized repression and hatred of the patriarchal culture. It isn’t real. I know all of it. People made it all up, and if we could all stop agreeing on it, things would be different. Gender is a construct. But, to quote Imogen Binnie, “Eventually you can’t help but figure out that, while gender is a construct, so is a traffic light, and if you ignore either of them, you get hit by cars.” Not being tangible doesn’t make rules less real.

If we’d grown up in a culture where we were taught women’s facial hair was beautiful, we’d all be applying medical creams under our noses and using moustache pencils. But we didn’t grow up in that culture. I hated my facial hair and I hated my penis even more. I thought it was incredibly ugly. I was one of those trans women who had looked at it and from that moment on showered in the dark. It made me sick. I pitied anyone who had to go down there.

I thought maybe transitioning might make me okay with it; that being seen as a woman and getting the facial hair zapped off would alleviate the pressure of hating myself for having a penis. But that just made the contrast sharper.

Yes, it started working differently. Yes, it got softer, and more delicate, and started smelling like pussy. One of the nice things about performing The Vagina Monologues is I get to come up here on stage and say actually yes, I really do like the smell of pussy. Yes I have heard the Contrapoints bit about the mouthfeel. But that didn’t make having a penis any easier.

Um, Natalie, on the off chance you see this and you want to demonstrate exactly how the mouthfeel changes, in person, here’s my number: ###-###-####.

So. In order to survive, I began to pretend there was nothing there. I imagined myself Barbie-doll smooth. Isn’t that a funny idiom? They’ve been printing underwear on Barbies since before I stole my older sisters’. Anyways I used a lot of wand vibrators and I did a lot of anal, always face down. Always with men.

Then I met C.

C was bisexual. She was short and thin and wore the kinds of things you would expect from somebody trying to make it clear to everybody that she was bisexual. I saw her get they’d once (she was giving she/they, though she wasn’t) and she took it as a compliment. She had a Lapidot charm on her keychain, if that means anything to you. I actually like Lapis a lot but it’s kind of a red flag. C did not like spicy foods or listen to anything but pop. Her favorite Asian cuisine was Japanese. She liked lingerie, especially on boys, and her tastes in BL ran to the shounen. She said what she thought, and apologized for it. She did not have any problems or issues and did not even drink. She wasn’t very funny or articulate or mysterious. She wasn’t mean or unavailable. She wasn’t self-involved or charismatic. She had a car with a bisexual flag sticker on the bumper, and she still took the bus.

I did not particularly like C. Actually I hated her immediately. I was jealous of her birdlike movements and the privileged ambivalence with which she performatively treated her own femininity. I would have missed her altogether if our fingers hadn’t touched when she pressed her number into my hand and ran back to her cheering friends. When we touched something happened. I told myself that it was just the novelty of a cis woman hitting on me but I ended up going to bed with her. That’s when the miracle occurred.

Turned out that C loved penises. She was a connoisseur. She loved the way they felt, the way they tasted, the way they smelled, but most importantly she loved the way they looked. She had to look at them. The first time we had sex, she told me she had to see me.

“I’m right here,” I said.

“No, you,” she said.

“I have to see you.”

“Turn on the light,” I said, thinking she was a weirdo and freaking out in the dark. Sure, a cis man could have killed me, but an allegation from a cis woman could cost me my job.

She turned on the light.

Then she said, “OK, I’m ready, ready to see you.”

“Right here,” I waved, “I’m right here.” I thought she was an idiot, and worse, I thought she was going to treat me like a man.

Then she began to undress me.

“What are you doing C?” I said.

“I need to see you,” she replied.

“No need,” I said. “Just do it.”

“I need to see what you look like,” she said.

“But you’ve seen a penis before,” I said.

“Of course I have,” she said. And then, anticipating my reply: “I have guy friends with benefits, you know. If I wanted a guy right now I would be with a guy right now,” confirming that I had not been her first trans woman, and that at least one of the previous ones had been comfortable enough with her to share her insecurities.

C continued. She would not stop. I wanted to throw up and die.

I held my breath. She looked and looked. She got breathy and her eyes went soft. I felt her eyes crawl upward to my breasts and up to my eyes and down again; out to my thighs and in again. Her gaze pressed through my skin like a new kind of touch.

“You’re so beautiful,” she said. “You’re elegant and deep and innocent and wild.”

It was like she read my palm.

“I saw that,” she said, “and more, much much more.”

She stayed looking for almost an hour as if she were studying a map, observing the moon, staring into my eyes, but it was my penis. In the light I watched her looking at me and she was so genuinely excited, so peaceful and euphoric, I began to get wet and turned on. I began to see myself the way she saw me. I began to feel beautiful and delicious — like a great painting, or a waterfall. C wasn’t afraid. She wasn’t grossed out. I began to swell, began to feel proud. Began to love my penis. And C lost herself there, and I was there with her, in my penis, and we were gone.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS:

(here’s Because He Liked To Look At It, in case you skipped it at the start)

Compare and contrast the weight of gendered expectations on cis women to the weight of gender dysphoria on trans women, particularly as each affects perceptions of the genitals.

Imagine a version of this story where a transgender woman helps a cisgender woman become more comfortable with her vagina. Does that read any differently? Should it?

All of the women were asked the following questions: If your penis got dressed what would it wear?

If your penis could talk, what would it say?

How many people are going to misread this post as evidence that I am trans? I am not trans.

Why can’t we get there? Why can’t we get to where that is and stop hurting each other? I want to go there. I want to go there and live there forever. Please. Why are we holding us back? Do you think we could get there someday?

title: A Part At The Seam: Recognizing Differences Between Cis And Trans Women
text:
Transgender women reading this article should be aware that topics likely to induce gender dysphoria will be discussed. I’m sorry, and I hope that transgender readers will take my history of allyship towards transgender women into account and give me what I deserve.

* * *

Do you ever think about how the worst word in the English language is a euphemism for the standard female genital configuration? I do. I think about it all the time. It explains a lot.

I was watching Lessons In Chemistry1, Starring Brie Larson as a plucky young chemist who is the only reasonable person in the world, because — even though the showrunners are clearly smearing the science in service of Christian moral arcs and don’t understand that Calvin Evans is clearly a gay man2 — anything where an intelligent woman3 who doesn’t need a diagnosis contends with the broken systems of a stupid and evil world is like candy to me.

Helen DeWitt keeps having problems with publishing and I saw the first half on a plane, okay?

Anyways Lessons in Chemistry ends with a very Pink victory: Elizabeth Zott manages to keep her show on air, in defiance of The Patriarchy Man, by scoring a Tampax sponsorship and giving a basic lecture on menstruation4. In the 1960s, when this show takes place, this would have been revolutionary; even in 2026 I teared up.

And yet. I couldn’t help but wonder how a transgender woman would feel, watching that.

Whether you’re a cis woman or a trans woman or even I guess one of the three or so men who read this blog for some reason5, you care about women. And if you care about women, you should already know about how estrogen-primacy affects heart attack symptoms, or how to perform a basic examination for possibly cancerous breast nodules — but did you know they were testing tampon absorbency with saline instead of blood until 2023? Not even saline with simulated clots. Straight saline. As a direct consequence of men and male bodies being considered the norm, female6 reproductive health is woefully understudied.

Trans women are women. They are subject to the social pressures that define women, have estrogen-primary hormonal systems, and conceive of themselves as women. This is as obvious without thought to me as it is for me to walk down the stairs.

And yet I would never ever take a trans woman to a production of The Vagina Monologues. Which is not to say that a transgender woman could not enjoy The Vagina Monologues7, just that I would feel really horrible about having the body part that people associate so definitively with womanhood sitting next to a woman who didn’t. It would be in terrible taste. I wouldn’t give somebody in remission a copy of The Emperor Of All Maladies either.

Clearly we need to be prioritizing research on/awareness of the standard XX reproductive system — and clearly we also need to prioritize the well-being of transgender women. The power of The Vagina Monologues is in the exposure and normalization of those things most women are raised to be ashamed of, and that power is fundamentally alienating to women with different bodies, raised under different paradigms of shame.

What do we do with this contradiction?

Well, we should prioritize the health of the majority. Women need to know how to manage our bodies. Let’s wear pussy hats, and get Tampax sponsorships, and celebrate the vagina as the wonderful if messy source of pleasure it has the potential to be. Maybe a bunch of straight women will come off as kind of lesbian for talking about pussy all the time but you know what, that’s fine. The really important thing is keeping women healthy and informed!

…This isn’t even wrong, but see how easy it is to forget about transgender women? How easy it is for even a devout feminist to abandon those women who need her most? No transgender woman is ever going to object to this, because that would mark her out as separate. She will sit in her room alone and cry and only ever spend time with other trans women.

We could try separating womanhood from the vagina. We could try referring to “birthing bodies” and gender-neutral pregnancy. This would also be nice for some nonbinary people. Unfortunately almost everybody who has ever tried to do this sounds unbearably woke, and not in a fun and clever way that makes people of all kinds feel welcome. I could do it, but most people are worse at writing than me, so it isn’t really a scalable solution.

We could try only talking to cis women about what are mostly cis woman’s issues8 , but setting up yet another women’s network that excludes transgender women is not the solution. It wouldn’t even work at scale, because most people aren’t capable of perfectly identifying trans women at a glance. Also this approach would attract TERFs.

We could, of course, do the thing that most women decide to do about it: ie; just buy their daughters The Care And Keeping Of You. Which, well. You could do worse.

We could take BB Wolfclaw’s route and elide the vagina by writing about women, both trans- and cis- gendered, who prefer anal. But I don’t think most of the world is ready for that. People are too busy being upset about vaginas to even begin to comprehend the feminist potentials of anal sex.

We could give all teens (not just girls. boys and nonbinary need to know about this too.) reasonable and comprehensive sex education. But apparently Christians have decided that they want girls to be confused and scared and in pain on their wedding nights, and apparently we as a country have decided that people who believe everything in a book they don’t even read all of are worth listening to for some reason.

Ultimately, I refuse to split the difference. I am unequivocally in favor of public reproductive health initiatives, and I am unequivocally in favor of transgender women, in the same ways as I am unequivocally in favor of the Earth our home remaining breathable and unequivocally in favor of airplane travel continuing to exist.

This second dichotomy does suggest a solution to the first. Just as we use carbon credits to offset the impact of transportation on our environments, I propose the use of transgender credits for offsetting the impact of reproductive health discussion on transgender women.

I realize that this sounds offputtingly libertarian of me, and for that I apologize.

Whenever I, as a cis woman, make some remark normalizing my vagina — and I have done so, and intend to keep doing so — I send a transgender woman I know ten dollars9 in compensation for emotional distress incurred. I refuse to prioritize my cisfeminism over my transfeminism, and I’m putting my money right where I want my mouth to be.

title: Give me the Infowars Byline.
text:
Hello Tim Heidecker, Soon-to-be Creative Director of Infowars,

Let me help you make your new website less transphobic. Transphilic, even.

A nonbinary person of my acquaintance has informed me that you are interested in turning Infowars into “the internet’s premier destination for transgender comedy.” If you’re serious about trans comedy, or you know literally anybody who is transgender, you know that no cisgender* person has ever managed to say anything funny about transgender people1.

*While many nonbinary people have certainly said funny things about transgender, definitive answers on whether nonbinary people as a demographic count as transgender have not been and may never be forthcoming. If I get an answer I will be sure to let you know.

With that lone qualification, I believe I am the first cisgender person ever to have said something funny about a transgender person. Consequently it is in your best interest to give me an Infowars byline.

If you don’t understand how this post is funny, you aren’t equipped to run a transgender comedy website.

You might note that there are a great number of very funny transgender women, nonbinary people, and men, to whom you intend to hire. Great! But transgender people say hilarious and cutting things to each other all the time — it’s just that nobody cisgender understands them. If you want to attract transgender comedians, you need to be catering to a trans audience; if you want to cater to a transgender audience, you need the first cisgender person to ever have said something funny2 about transgender people.

Me.

Awaiting your reply,

Halimede.

Perhaps, Tim Heidecker, you want to receive more of my emails. or even compensate me monetarily for them. via this link.

title: A Cisgender Woman And A Transgender Woman Play A Game Of Magic The Gathering
text:
* * *

Here is what they each noticed about each other when they sat down:

The transgender woman didn’t seem to know when to make or not make eye contact. She had a few dice on the table, which would be very useful; the cisgender woman regretted not bringing her own. Hopefully she would be offered some. The transgender woman looked like she spent a lot of time online but in the way where she had clearly spent at least some of it figuring out individual pieces of her look, if not how they were intended to fit together. Shaggy black 80’s hair; high-collar ribbed halter top, to show off her arms; round-rimmed glasses. No makeup. She had pianist’s fingers, with deep-green shimmery nails, which she kept rubbing up against each other nail to nail; and a low and quiet voice, with which she had been chatting about how new cards related to old cards with the man sitting beside her when the cisgender woman sat down for the round. The cisgender woman waited for them to stop talking to each other and when the transgender woman was facing her she gave her a little wave and her name and asked her if she was there often. She was happy to not be playing against a man.

The cisgender woman didn’t seem to know what she was doing. Which was fine; it wasn’t a competitive event. Everybody here was here for the kind of fun that involved looking at and showing off new cards and being delighted by the ways they fit together and chatting and not necessarily for the kind of fun where two people test lies against math until one of them loses, which there would be plenty of time for later. The transgender woman was a little jealous of the way that she filled out her dress, and of her ability to wear boat necklines, and more than a little jealous of the fact that the cisgender woman would be given the correct pronouns no matter what, and of the ways she had been raised etc. Her shoulder-length hair was down and wavy, and she was staring at the transgender woman in a way that the transgender woman understood to be incredibly judgmental. In order to avoid this stare the transgender woman replied to the man sitting next to her, who she otherwise would probably have ignored.

When she had finished talking with him, the transgender woman replied to the cisgender woman with her name and the fact that this was her third time at that particular game store. Then she pulled out her phone and opened a score counter app, not having realized that the cisgender woman had already done the same thing. Ah, said the cisgender woman, we can do it like that, by which she meant that it was fine with her if the two of them used separate phones to track their scores. Oh, said the transgender woman, I didn’t realize you already had your phone out. The cisgender woman picked her phone up because she had just realized that she hadn’t muted her notifications and she did not particularly want to hear from one of her friends, who was still her friend but who had a bad habit of texting her things that she wouldn’t have wanted anybody else to see at moments that other people would see them. The transgender woman said that she was fine with just using hers for both, as she assumed the cisgender woman had indicated by picking up her phone, even though that had not been her intention. The cisgender woman did not want to challenge the transgender woman, so she said that was fine. And so they ended up using the transgender woman’s phone.

* * *

Here is how they played:

The cisgender woman had assembled a deck around the accretion of various lasting pieces, each of which improved with the addition of others. Her position improved with the length of the game. She played hesitantly, asking before every action, as she did not want to mess up or make the transgender woman uncomfortable.

The transgender woman had assembled a fiddly and specific deck requiring a lot of game knowledge, particularly in relation to threat assessment, and effects that lasted for only a turn. She was in large part playing against herself. She played quickly, because she had all the time that the cisgender woman was taking on her turn to think of her next moves, and because she was decisive, at least in games.

However, although the transgender woman made no secret of preferring the kind of fun where two people test lies against math until one of them loses, she did not want to beat the cisgender woman. She was in fact mildly annoyed with the cisgender woman’s unsure pace, though she thought she hid that well. She cared quite a lot about the cisgender woman’s feelings, or at least about what she thought of her, and so she made moves that were less than perfect, because she did not want the cisgender woman to feel like she had not had a chance to win. Because of this, and because of the strengths and weaknesses of the decks they had assembled, specifically re: gaining advantage over time, and because of the variance inherent in card games, the cisgender woman won the first of three rounds.

She apologized for this. The transgender woman said what are you apologizing for? You won. This made the cisgender woman a bit uncomfortable, because she was just apologizing because she didn’t want the transgender woman to feel bad.

* * *

At this point they had already developed slightly unflattering assumptions about each other.

The transgender woman assumed that the cisgender woman was there with her boyfriend; though the transgender woman herself was exclusively sexually romantically etc interested in women, the presumption that the cisgender woman was straight (which the cisgender woman did, incidentally, happen to be) and, not unrelatedly, better at performing womanhood than she was, put her on the defensive immediately. Actually the cisgender woman’s older brother had introduced her to the game when they were teens together, because a girl he had a crush on was playing it1. She had never been amazing at it but winning had never been the point; and besides if she had won her brother would have hidden it but it would have hurt his teen boy pride. And she had very fond memories of the art, and of feeling like a powerful witch summoning and empowering monsters from her spellbook.

The cisgender woman assumed that the transgender woman was judging her. Which she was. But she assumed, being herself insecure and covering that up by asking exactly when game actions could be performed even when she thought they could be etc, that she was being judged for playing badly. The transgender woman was actually judging her for her lack of confidence. The transgender woman only found zero-sum games fun when both players wanted to be there, and while the cisgender woman wanted to be there, the transgender woman assumed that she did not because of the ways in which she was playing.

* * *

The transgender woman won the second game quickly and decisively, because she was a much more experienced player and because of the fact that the cisgender woman drew all her cards in the wrong order. Good game, said the cisgender woman, even though she had lost. I’m sorry it wasn’t, said the transgender woman. What she meant was that she was sorry that the game hadn’t been particularly exciting or technical, and what the cisgender woman understood was that the transgender woman was very committed to honesty when perhaps other virtues might better serve her and those around her.

On the second turn of their third game the cisgender woman played an incredibly powerful card which the transgender woman did not think was allowed. When she expressed surprise, the man sitting next to her informed her that there was a 1 in 55 pack chance of opening one of the ten cards of which this was one, and that 1 in 550 was a statistical inevitability with a large enough data set. Which she knew. Still, though.

This very powerful card did something very powerful that resulted in the cisgender woman winning the third game, for which she apologized again. I wish you wouldn’t apologize so much, said the transgender woman. You won! The cisgender woman could see that she was a little upset still but of course she did not say anything. What could she have said to that? She thanked her for the games and they moved on to play against men.

Neither of them ever went back to that game store again.

* * *

That night the cisgender woman sat alone in her apartment eating Thai takeout and trying not to think about her recent breakup. Elsewhere the transgender woman nestled in the crook of her transgender girlfriend’s arm. I wish I got along better with cis women, the transgender woman said. I played against one today but she just didn’t get it. Or I didn’t. Or both of those things probably. I wish I had cis girl friends.

Her girlfriend kissed her on the forehead. They’re just weird, she said. We’re better off without them.

Isn’t that kind of awful to say, said the transgender girl. She was trying her best. Or as best as she was capable of, or allowed herself to be capable of.

Maybe, said the transgender girl’s girlfriend. But if you want more magic, you know who will play with you. Get your deck out.

* * *

Never ever ask me to write about magic gambling ever again.

With thanks to magic the gathering consultants C. B. and M, without whom I would have had to learn things about magic the gathering
